profileSection.badge: Software Engineer · Full Stack & DevOps · Ecuador
paragraphs: I started coding at 14 out of curiosity about how video games are made. That question led me to algorithms, then to software engineering, and eventually to building systems that run in production for real teams.

Today I work at the intersection of web development, infrastructure automation, and DevOps. I'm in my element when a well-designed solution eliminates repetitive work and gives people their time back. Lately I've been incorporating AI Agents and Gen AI into that flow, a direction I find genuinely exciting.
Outside of code, I enjoy anime, watching video game analysis, and keep on learning, whether through a course, a paper, or just breaking things in the home lab.

activities: Identified automation opportunities in critical operations and designed and implemented 10+ end-to-end workflows that eliminated repetitive tasks consuming hours of the team's time each day.
Developed an internal Python library that I proposed as the team standard, establishing shared patterns and reducing development time for new automations.

Took the initiative to design and build from scratch an internal platform that centralizes and automates key department processes, with role-based access control. Full ownership project, currently in use by the operations team.
Built web systems with Vue.js and Node.js, delivering multiple REST endpoints serving internal users across operations and engineering.
Worked with the team to design and implement a web platform that replaced manual Excel-based processes, giving the company real-time operational visibility for the first time.
Took full ownership of the backend with FastAPI and PostgreSQL, building the database and RESTful APIs that support business-critical operations.
Collaborated closely with the frontend team on dashboard redesigns, improving user experience and information clarity.

activities: Part of a team of 10 engineers distributed across Latin America, collaborating remotely and asynchronously under agile methodologies to maintain and evolve a multinational logistics platform.
Developed and shipped new features with React and Node.js, directly contributing to the operational continuity of the product in production.
Participated in the implementation of low-latency transactions using Redis, ensuring system performance in critical real-time operations.

Worked with Clojure in a production billing system, gaining hands-on experience with functional programming paradigms.

Taught algorithm analysis, guiding students through exercises and problem-solving strategies.

Developed educational materials and provided individualized support.

projects.title: ani-scrapy
projects.tagline: Python scraping library published on PyPI
projects.shortDescription: Unified abstract interface for multiple anime sources.

narrative.problem: I watch anime regularly but the titles I follow are rarely on streaming platforms, so I end up searching for them on alternative sites. The problem: aggressive ads at every step, multiple download servers to try, and 25 to 45 seconds wasted per episode just waiting for ads to pass. Multiplied across a long anime like One Piece, that becomes completely unviable.
narrative.approach: I started with a loose Python script using Playwright, which I chose over Selenium because it was more modern and straightforward. At first it was unstable: dynamic rendering and ad handling kept failing. I iterated: added retry logic, integrated Stealth, and switched to the Brave browser to evade bot detection. The breaking point came when I wanted to add a second site, my code broke because everything was tied to the first one. That's when I decided to extract it as a library with a common interface, so switching or adding a source wouldn't be a headache. To close the loop, I set up a GitHub Actions pipeline that automatically publishes a new version to PyPI on every release, anyone can install it with a simple `pip install`.
narrative.learned: I learned to scrape in hostile environments: aggressive ads, bot detection, and dynamic rendering that changes without warning. I also understood firsthand why interface design matters in libraries, a poorly designed interface from the start charges you the bill when you try to extend the system. And that publishing to PyPI is not just uploading code: it requires thinking about versioning, compatibility, and documentation as if someone else were going to use it.

projects.title: Ani Seek
projects.tagline: Full stack app with custom scraping and automated deployment
projects.shortDescription: Web interface to search, browse, and parallel-download anime. Built on top of ani-scrapy.

narrative.problem: ani-scrapy solved the downloading, but using it was still a developer thing: calling functions manually, handling complex data structures in the console, no way to queue downloads or track which episodes I already had. I wanted something anyone could use without touching a single line of code.
narrative.approach: The goal was clear: a web interface with good UX that abstracted everything ani-scrapy did under the hood. I used technologies I already knew to focus on the new logic. For download progress bars I started with constant polling, I knew it was inefficient but it was quick to implement. While researching I discovered SSE, which turned out to be exactly what I needed: the server pushes real-time updates without the overhead of WebSockets. For the downloads themselves, which are heavy processes, I implemented work queues, first with Celery, then migrated to Dramatiq as a more modern and simpler alternative. Deployment was another learning experience: it was the first project I deployed on my home lab with a full pipeline, change verification, Docker image build and publish, and a webhook to Dokploy that triggers the deployment automatically.
narrative.learned: I learned that choosing the right tool for real-time communication matters: polling works, but SSE is the elegant solution when data flows in only one direction. Also that work queues are not just an architectural detail, without them a long download would block the entire application. And perhaps most valuable: closing the full cycle of a project, from code to automated deployment in production, gives you a perspective you can't get any other way.

projects.title: Home Lab
projects.shortDescription: Local server + Oracle VPS. Full self-hosted and containerized stack.

narrative.problem: There was no problem to solve, there was an unused mini PC and a desire to learn. I wanted my own place to deploy projects, experiment with technologies, and run apps I use daily like Immich, Jellyfin, n8n, or a Minecraft server, without depending on external services.
narrative.approach:
I started with CasaOS because it was the most accessible option for someone new to self-hosting: clean interface and a marketplace that abstracted all Docker Compose configuration. It worked well for standard apps, but as soon as I tried to deploy Ani Seek I hit its limits: not enough flexibility for custom solutions and very basic monitoring. I migrated to Dokploy, which was more developer-oriented: automated deployment pipelines, environment variable management, real-time logs, and full custom Docker Compose support.

For public exposure, my first approach was Cloudflare Tunnels, manually creating each subdomain pointing directly to the container port. It worked, but it wouldn't scale. I then got a free VPS on Oracle and a free domain with DigitalPlat. When I tried to apply Cloudflare Tunnels on the VPS, the documentation clarified it wasn't necessary since the VPS already has a public IP, and along the way I discovered how to configure it correctly: point the tunnel to Traefik and let Dokploy handle subdomain routing. Today I have two Dokploy instances, one public with direct IP and one private with Cloudflare Tunnels, each with its own domain.
narrative.learned: I learned that self-hosting exposes you to everything managed platforms resolve without you noticing: networking, reverse proxies, certificates, log management. That reading the actual documentation, not just hunting for the fastest tutorial, sometimes saves you from unnecessary architectures. And that a home lab is not just infrastructure: it's the place where concepts you learn in courses or at work become real.

projects.title: PPL Adventure
projects.tagline: Unity game built for the TAWS Club admission process
projects.shortDescription: 2D Unity game set on the ESPOL campus. Mentored the team through execution.

narrative.problem: TAWS Club needed a project for its admission process that tested how well new candidates could execute under guidance. The challenge was designing something with enough scope to be completed in the available time, but complex enough to reveal how candidates think and collaborate.
narrative.approach: I designed the game concept and guided the team through execution rather than building it myself. The game is set on the ESPOL campus and developed with Unity and C#. My role was to define the scope, unblock the team when they hit technical obstacles, and ensure project delivery, not write the code.
narrative.learned: Being a mentor is a different skill from building. The impulse to just solve a problem yourself is counterproductive when your goal is to help someone else learn how to do it. I got better at asking questions that lead the team toward the solution rather than giving it directly.

projects.title: Subnetting
projects.shortDescription: Web tool for IP segmentation using FLSM and VLSM techniques.

narrative.problem: Subnet calculations are tedious to do by hand and existing tools had poor UX. It was also one of my first projects with React and Next.js, so the challenge was as much about learning the stack as building something useful.
narrative.approach: I implemented the FLSM and VLSM algorithms and built a static web interface in Next.js to expose them. The focus was on presenting results clearly, a step-by-step breakdown so the user understands the process, not just gets a number.
narrative.learned: This was my first real encounter with component-based thinking in React. Looking at it now, the code is more imperative than it should be. I would restructure it with better separation between calculation logic and UI state. Even so, it was the project that made frontend click for me.

projects.title: Urbapass Backend
projects.tagline: REST API for access control in residential complexes
projects.shortDescription: Access control backend managing residents, visitors, and entry records.

narrative.problem: Urbapass needed a backend to manage access control in a residential complex, residents, visitors, entry records, and notifications. The challenge was designing a data model flexible enough to handle different types of users and access rules.
narrative.approach: I built a RESTful API with Node.js and Express, using MySQL for relational data (users, units, access rules) and MongoDB for records and events that didn't fit a rigid schema. JWT handled authentication and Sequelize served as the ORM for the relational side.
narrative.learned: Using two databases in the same project taught me to think carefully about what data goes where. I over-engineered parts of the MySQL schema early on and had to refactor. I would start with a simpler schema and evolve it, premature normalization is just as problematic as its absence.
